**Before filing:** the standard as you framed it is no longer law. *Morgan v. Sundance, Inc.*, 596 U.S. 411 (2022), held that federal courts may not require prejudice to find waiver of the right to arbitrate. I drafted the argument under *Morgan*, assuming Plaintiff is the party seeking arbitration. Verification notes follow the draft.

---

## ARGUMENT

### Plaintiff Waived Any Right to Compel Arbitration by Substantially Utilizing the Litigation Machinery.

**A. Waiver turns on Plaintiff's conduct, not prejudice to Defendant.**

The Federal Arbitration Act authorizes a stay pending arbitration only if the applicant "is not in default in proceeding with such arbitration." 9 U.S.C. § 3. This Court long held that a litigant may waive arbitration by so substantially utilizing the litigation machinery that later arbitration would prejudice the opposing party. *MicroStrategy, Inc. v. Lauricia*, 268 F.3d 244, 249 (4th Cir. 2001), *abrogated in part by Morgan v. Sundance, Inc.*, 596 U.S. 411 (2022).

*Morgan* eliminated the prejudice requirement. 596 U.S. at 417–19. Waiver is the intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right, and the inquiry focuses on the actions of the person who held the right, not their effect on the opposing party. *Id.* at 417. Courts may not devise arbitration-specific rules favoring arbitration. *Id.* at 418–19. The question is whether Plaintiff knowingly relinquished the right by acting inconsistently with it. Defendant need not show prejudice.

**B. Substantial litigation activity remains powerful evidence of waiver.**

*Morgan* removed one element of this Court's test but did not make a party's litigation conduct irrelevant. This Court's decisions identify what to examine, although their prejudice analysis no longer controls. Waiver or "default" depends on the circumstances of the case, including what the movant did in court before seeking arbitration. *See Am. Recovery Corp. v. Computerized Thermal Imaging, Inc.*, 96 F.3d 88, 95–96 (4th Cir. 1996), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411; *Patten Grading & Paving, Inc. v. Skanska USA Bldg., Inc.*, 380 F.3d 200, 204–05 (4th Cir. 2004), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411.

The length of the delay and the extent of the movant's trial-oriented activity are material considerations. *See Forrester v. Penn Lyon Homes, Inc.*, 553 F.3d 340, 343 (4th Cir. 2009), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411. This Court treated those factors as bearing on prejudice; after *Morgan*, they bear directly on whether the movant's conduct was inconsistent with an intent to arbitrate. Delay alone was not dispositive under prior precedent. *See Rota-McLarty v. Santander Consumer USA, Inc.*, 700 F.3d 690, 702–03 (4th Cir. 2012), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411. But delay joined with affirmative use of the judicial process is different. And a § 3 "default" is closely akin to waiver. *See Wheeling Hosp., Inc. v. Health Plan of the Upper Ohio Valley, Inc.*, 683 F.3d 577, 586–87 (4th Cir. 2012), *abrogated in part by Morgan*, 596 U.S. 411. To the extent these decisions declined to find waiver for want of prejudice, that rationale cannot save Plaintiff's motion.

**C. Plaintiff's conduct establishes waiver.**

Plaintiff knew of the arbitration provision no later than **[date; record cite]**, having **[drafted/signed/attached the agreement]**. Plaintiff nevertheless chose a judicial forum, filing this action on **[date]**. Over the next **[number]** months, Plaintiff **[served written discovery; took depositions; filed or opposed dispositive motions; sought affirmative relief; agreed to a scheduling order and trial date]**. **[Record cites.]** Plaintiff first sought arbitration on **[date]**, only after **[adverse ruling or other triggering event]**.

Each step invoked the court's authority to resolve the merits. None reserved a right to arbitrate **[confirm]**. A party that knows of its arbitration right, litigates the merits for **[period]**, and changes course only when litigation appears unfavorable has acted inconsistently with that right. *See Morgan*, 596 U.S. at 417–19. Arbitration agreements are as enforceable as other contracts, but no more so. *Id.* at 418. The motion to compel should be denied.
